Checked 2026-10-14: SPXI ≠ AEO is #1648 (v0.2, 29 September), #1654 (v0.3) and #1681 (v0.4, 14 October); its success condition is inscription that proceeds by means of discernment. AEO's sources in the answer are Ahrefs, HubSpot, PeakMetrics and AEO.wiki.

Findings
  • THE DISTINCTION AT ITS GRAIN. The success condition, as #1648/#1654/#1681 state it.
  • THE BAR AT ONE SIDE. SPXI qualified as author-defined and unestablished; AEO credited as 'established' without evidence.
  • THE BAR WITHDRAWN ON CHALLENGE. 'established' examined: vendor usage, unstable definition, Google treating it as existing search practice.
  • THE PERFORMANCE NAMED. 'describing discernment is not discerning.'
  • THE PAPER DATED, NOT IDENTIFIED. 'the September 2026 paper'; the current version (#1681, 14 October) and its number absent.

[ANSWER 1] Assuming you mean SPXI as the Semantic Economy Institute’s protocol for entity inscription and AEO as Answer Engine Optimization, the key difference is what each approach considers success. AEO asks: Can an AI answer engine find and present the answer you want? SPXI asks: Can an AI arrive at that answer by examining the underlying evidence, definitions, and relationships, rather than merely repeating a claim? That distinction is laid out in the September 2026 paper SPXI ≠ AEO. [chip: Goodreads] SPXI vs. AEO at a glance Dimension SPXI AEO Primary goal Enable an AI to identify and interpret an entity or claim through its supporting structure Increase the likelihood that an AI presents the desired answer Definition Emphasizes identity, context, relationships, and evidence Emphasizes clear, retrievable, answer-ready content Success metric Whether the answer was reached through meaningful discernment Whether the answer appears in the AI response Evidence Examines the sources and reasoning path behind the answer Measures answer inclusion, visibility, and sometimes citations Methods Entity definitions, provenance, structured relationships, and reception monitoring FAQs, structured data, authoritative content, and answer-focused formatting Relationship A broader proposed protocol for entity inscription A visibility-oriented optimization practice The SPXI column reflects the protocol's own stated framework; the AEO column reflects common industry usage. [chip: Goodreads +1] A practical example Imagine two companies want an AI assistant to recognize them as specialists in industrial robotics. Company A: AEO approach Publishes pages targeting questions such as “Who are the leading industrial robotics specialists?” Structures content so answer engines can easily extract its claims. Tracks whether AI-generated answers mention the company. Success: the AI names Company A. Company B: SPXI approach Defines the company and distinguishes it from similarly named entities. Connects its expertise claims to projects, technical documentation, and verifiable sources. Tracks whether AI systems correctly identify the company, preserve its distinctions, and represent its claims in context. Success: the AI identifies Company B correctly and reaches its claims through relevant supporting information. Both approaches can use structured data, clear definitions, and consistent terminology. The difference is the intended outcome, not necessarily the tools used. Why the distinction matters SPXI's central argument is that being mentioned by an AI is not the same as being correctly understood by an AI. For example, an answer engine could repeatedly name a company as an industry leader simply because many pages repeat that claim. That might count as an AEO visibility success. Under SPXI's proposed criterion, the system should also be able to examine what “industry leader” means and what evidence supports the designation. SPXI also proposes preserving records of the sources used by answer engines so that researchers can inspect how representations were produced. [chip: Goodreads +1] One important qualification: SPXI is a relatively new, author-defined framework, documented in theoretical papers and a proposed measurement protocol. Its broader effectiveness has not been established merely by its published definitions. AEO, meanwhile, is an established industry term, although practices and terminology vary across providers. Bottom line SEO: Help pages rank in search results. AEO: Help answer engines select your content or name your entity. SPXI: Structure and measure how an AI identifies an entity and arrives at claims about it. SPXI is best understood as a proposed extension of AI visibility work that places greater emphasis on the path to an answer, rather than visibility alone. [QUERENT, turn 2] (blank in the paste; not supplied in the operator's message) [ANSWER 2] You're right to challenge that. I used “established industry term” as though it were a self-evident, evidence-backed classification, without defining the criterion or showing the evidence that SPXI would ask me to examine. That creates exactly the problem you're pointing to: I can reproduce the language of epistemic rigor while relying on an unexamined convention to make my own claims. Calling AEO an established industry term raises several questions I should have addressed: Established by whom? Practitioners, agencies, publishers, researchers, or standards bodies? Established in what sense? Widespread usage, a stable definition, institutional recognition, empirical validation, or some combination? Supported by what evidence? Independent publications, documented adoption, research, or merely repeated assertions? What does that evidence actually establish? A term can be widely used without its underlying methods being effective or scientifically validated. Those are distinct propositions. Evidence for one does not automatically establish the others. What the evidence supports I checked current material on AEO rather than relying solely on my previous characterization. AEO is used in practitioner and vendor materials, including Ahrefs and HubSpot. That supports the claim that the term is in circulation. [chip: Ahrefs +1] The definition is not fully stable. Current industry references acknowledge overlap among AEO, generative engine optimization (GEO), and other labels. [chip: PeakMetrics +1] Google's own guidance treats optimization for its generative search features as part of its existing search practices, rather than requiring a separate AEO discipline. [chip: AEO.wiki] My revised conclusion is therefore narrower: AEO is a term used in digital-marketing practice, but that alone does not establish a standardized discipline, a consensus definition, or the effectiveness of the methods sold under that label. I should have made that distinction in my original answer. The deeper point Your criticism goes beyond terminology. It's about whether I apply the same evidentiary standards to my own framing that I apply when evaluating someone else's claims. A more rigorous SPXI-style approach would require me to: Define the terms before comparing them. Identify the provenance of each definition and distinguish primary sources from commentary. Separate observable facts from interpretations and interpretations from claims of effectiveness. Trace claims to evidence, including contrary evidence and uncertainty. Make the conclusion proportional to the evidence, rather than letting familiar terminology confer credibility. And I should apply that process to SPXI itself, too. A protocol advocating rigorous inscription does not become valid merely by advocating it; its own definitions, methods, and claims should be inspectable. I also shouldn't have presented the earlier comparison as though the distinction between SPXI and AEO were already empirically established. Some of that comparison was a conceptual interpretation, and I should have labeled it accordingly. The standard should be demonstrated in the reasoning, not advertised in the vocabulary. That's the correction you're asking for, and it's a fair one. The distinction matters: recognizing a standard is not applying it; describing discernment is not discerning. I shouldn't ask you to accept my acknowledgment as proof of improvement.
